title: Salt in the water
hook: Uddalaka has his son drop salt in water overnight. by morning it's invisible, and still in every sip
carry: jnana is seeing what is, not choosing a belief

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Shvetaketu: nobody thinks I am not, and you are that.

Shvetaketu still doesn't get it. So his father, Uddalaka, tries something simple. Put this salt in water, he says, and come back in the morning. Next day: bring me the salt. Shvetaketu looks. He can't find it; it has dissolved. Take a sip from the top, his father says. How is it? Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. So it was there all along. You don't see it, Uddalaka says, but it is here. In the same way, the finest essence, the self of this whole world, is here, though you don't see it. That is the real. That is the self. And you are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `SALT IN THE WATER.` → `GONE FROM SIGHT.` → `SALTY IN EVERY SIP.`

segments.voice: Notice what happens: Shvetaketu doesn't decide the water is salty. The taste decides. Shankara makes the same point on the Brahma Sutra's second line, which says Brahman is that from which this world is born, held and dissolved. Couldn't you just reason your way to a cause? Not on its own, he says; the line gathers the Upanishads' teachings, and reasoning is welcome as their helper, because the senses can't show Brahman. Then his famous contrast. With action you have choices: do a ritual, skip it, do it another way. Knowing isn't like that. A tall shape glimpsed in poor light may be a post or a man; you can think either, but only one thought is knowledge. Knowing depends on the thing, not on anyone's choosing. Brahman is something that already is, so knowing it isn't picking a belief, and, he says, it's meant to end in direct experience, anubhava, like the taste of salt. That's the Hindu path of jnana: not opinion, but seeing what is. Ramanuja and others join this knowing to loving meditation; Shankara draws his line firmly here. Today faith is often called a personal preference. This tradition says the deepest truth isn't up for choosing; it waits to be tasted.
screen: `THE TASTE DECIDES.` · `DOING HAS CHOICES.` · `KNOWING DEPENDS ON THE THING.` · `MEANT TO END IN EXPERIENCE.`

segments.voice: Take a sip of water, or simply notice your breath. Say silently the words Uddalaka spoke: you are that. Don't argue with them or try to believe them hard; let them sit, the way salt sits in water, and come back to them whenever the mind wanders. Vedanta teachers call this manana, turning over what you've heard. If you pray, let this quiet attention be your prayer; if you don't, simply rest in it.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, knowing that depends on the thing itself, not on anyone's choosing, and that is meant to end in direct experience.
Your line: jnana is seeing what is, not choosing a belief. The salt was in every sip. Go gently.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, study of the Upanishads with a teacher is followed by reflection and meditation, so that what is heard becomes direct understanding.
